statement: Wireframe visual conventions double as the design's non-colour cues so every signal remains legible without colour.
why: Ensures no information relies on colour alone.

statement: Selection and 'now' are encoded as an amber outline (#FFB301), the sole saturated attention channel (wireframe cue: ▐ … ▌).
why: Reserves saturated amber strictly for current focus and selection.

statement: Facts stated in the workbook file use solid lines and plain names in ink (#353938) and teal (#318995) for structure.
why: Distinguishes workbook truth from program inference.

statement: Items inferred by the program rather than stated in the file use dashed teal lines and guillemet labels ‹label›.
why: Makes inference visibly distinct from file-stored facts.

statement: Proposed or previewed items not yet in the file appear as ghosts using dotted teal lines and slanted/casual type.
why: Separates uncommitted previews and proposals from committed workbook state.

statement: Errors are marked by a red tick (#D02A23) on the cell's left edge alongside Excel's error text; red means nothing else.
why: Keeps red unambiguous and leaves the cell's own formatting untouched.

statement: Cells fed from outside data or volatile functions carry the ◊ glyph in signal orange (#FF8001, text #A35400).
why: Makes external links, RTD, add-ins and volatility immediately visible.

statement: Values changed in the most recent recalculation show a fading green underline (#3F8B76) (wireframe cue: •).
why: Gives transient feedback on what moved after recalculation.

statement: Warnings have no colour hue of their own and use bold ink with a hollow triangle ([!]).
why: Avoids adding another hue to the signal palette.

statement: Cast workbook reference figures are pinned across mockups: Budget 2027 (Base rev 3,940,602 / costs 3,017,387 / op profit 923,215; Downside 3,255,671 / 2,689,858 / 565,813), Sales (Report!D9 1,204,318.50 vs Pivot 1,251,907.25), Loan (250,000 at 6.50% / 30y, payment 1,580.17), Stock (Store.Stock, Supply.ReorderPoint, 1 pass/recalc), Inherited.xls (40 sheets, 301,482 formulas, Curves A1:IV900, 2/5 links missing, Module1, 4,226 errors from 3 roots, manual calc).
why: Ensures consistent, verifiable numbers across every mockup and test script.
evidence: Cast workbooks: Budget, Sales, Loan, Stock, Inherited

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Fable adds petrol-800-scoped chrome ink tokens (--c-ink #EDF1F2, --c-meta #A9C0C7, --c-teal #4FC0D8, --c-green #74C7AB, --c-ext #F0A35C, --c-red #FF9C96, --c-const #7DB8D8) on top of Strand's cockpit-light tokens because Strand specifies ink variants for dark paper but not for petrol-800 chrome.
why: Maintains contrast for signal inks rendered on dark petrol chrome bands.

statement: Three dressed component renders illustrate the live visual grammar: cell states on paper (typed constants in constant ink, amber selection with fill handle, green underline for fresh, red left tick for errors, signal orange ◊ for external, diagonal hatch for as-saved, dotted teal italic for ghost), line-style truth chips (solid name, dashed inferred label, dotted ghost, amber active caret), and the always-present petrol Strip.
why: Shows how the wireframe symbols translate to styled surfaces and contrast-checked tokens.

statement: 'Modern on the surface' does not mean new paint on a grid, fewer features, or decorative animation; it means four concrete capabilities Excel's surface omits.
why: Anchors modernisation in user-visible clarity and honesty rather than cosmetic styling.

statement: Structure is visible: blocks, runs of like formulas, names, tables and flows are read from the file and shown as selectable objects to point at.
why: Makes hidden spreadsheet architecture legible without manual annotation.

statement: State is visible: calculation status, errors and their roots, uncalculated values, outside data and change provenance are standing instruments rather than modal dialogs.
why: Keeps truth about the workbook continuously visible instead of buried in pop-ups.

statement: Consequences come before commitment: every edit previews what it will write to the file before Enter (the preview seam), and Esc is an exact revert.
why: Prevents silent model damage from edits made in higher-level views or Classic.

statement: The reader picks the surface: five views show one workbook to five kinds of reader while the file stays plain Excel and the grid remains one key away.
why: Matches presentation to task without splitting the underlying workbook or locking out Classic.

statement: Honesty is a hard constraint rather than a weighted quality: no view may show a value, formula, dependency or state unsupported by Excel-faithful calculation; views that simplify must say so in place with counts, and views that cannot be truthful must decline with a way forward.
why: Prevents misleading simplifications across all views.

statement: Quality priorities differ by view under the honesty constraint: Classic ranks familiarity > density > clarity; Inspector and Model map rank clarity > density > familiarity; Notebook ranks clarity > familiarity > density; App ranks clarity > familiarity with the task > density.
why: Resolves trade-offs cleanly for each persona and view.

statement: Outside Classic, familiarity means preserving Excel's formula language, editing keys and terminology rather than copying the grid layout.
why: Lets non-grid views stay intuitive to Excel users without imitating spreadsheet chrome.

statement: Every view shares one shell built from Strand's Mast, Bridge and Strip plus a single-row command Deck.
why: Prevents the five views from feeling like five separate applications.

statement: Every view shares one selection, one address field in Excel terms, and one formula bar where F2 edits the selected item's formula with all Classic formula keys.
why: Guarantees continuity of place and editing skill across views.

statement: Every view shares one edit grammar (type to replace, F2 to edit, Enter to commit, Esc to revert, Tab to commit and move), and SELECTED vs EDITING states show simultaneously in three places: the item, the formula bar, and the Strip.
why: Eliminates mode confusion across views.

statement: Every view uses one unified signal vocabulary: amber for now, red for error, signal orange for outside/volatile data, green for fresh, teal for structure, each paired with a shape, plus line style (solid stated, dashed inferred, dotted ghost) as a second channel.
why: Ensures consistent interpretation and accessibility without relying on colour alone.

statement: Every view shares one peek card, one set of docked panels (Details, Trace, Changes, Issues, Outline, Watch), one workbook undo history, one command palette (Alt+Q), and one Esc ladder that steps back exactly one level.
why: Keeps auxiliary tools and escape behaviour predictable everywhere.

statement: Excel's shortcuts remain untouched; all ten DNA Calc-specific shortcuts live on the Alt+Shift layer: 1-5 for views, 0 for grid alongside, L for lens, E for Formula Explorer, T for Trace, and D for Details.
why: Avoids colliding with Excel muscle memory while keeping new capabilities easy to remember.

statement: The shared shell (M0.1) comprises seven regions: (1) Mast with file/state, five view tabs, and unified 'Ask or run… (Alt+Q)' field; (2) one-row Deck using Excel tab names and key-tip letters in DNA Calc styling; (3) Bridge with address field and formula bar (folded by default only in App); (4) paper Stage with the shared selection; (5) right/bottom docked Panel (Details = pinned peek card); (6) Sheet tabs in Classic (sections/pages/levels elsewhere); (7) never-hidden Strip showing mode, calc, errors, outside data, macros, agent, and statistics.
why: Provides a single, stable spatial frame across all five views.

statement: P1 (Truth before polish, highest precedence): simplify only visibly and decline rather than fake — e.g., draw a delay only where the system reports a last-pass read, show errors and causes on App tiles rather than blanks, report run exceptions as '11 alike, 1 differs', and label saved values 'as saved'.
why: Gives a deterministic tie-breaker when clarity or polish conflicts with honesty.

statement: P2 (One workbook, one pointer): selection, address, clipboard and undo belong to the workbook rather than to any view, so switching views never loses place and Ctrl+[/Ctrl+] mean upstream/downstream everywhere.
why: Keeps all views synchronized views of one underlying model.

statement: P3 (Every edit is an Excel edit, previewed): any model-changing gesture previews the exact cells, names or settings it will write, must be reproducible in Excel, and undoes as one step; non-model gestures are free presentation or refused (e.g., notebook sort is a view sort, prose quotes values without computing, sliders commit on release so iteration ticks once, App scenarios are Excel scenarios).
why: Protects round-trip compatibility with Excel and makes side effects explicit.

statement: P4 (Read the file first, ask second, always allow correction): the program infers blocks, labels, inputs and patterns automatically with visible evidence and confidence, stores corrections with the file, and never requires upfront declarations before a view works.
why: Makes views immediately useful on existing ordinary Excel files.

statement: P5 (Old hands lose nothing): Classic honours every Appendix A Excel gesture unchanged (e.g., Ctrl+` stays Show Formulas while lens takes Alt+Shift+L, Alt+Q opens the palette, key-tip paths preserve Excel letters), and no skin may lock the grid away.
why: Protects decades of Excel muscle memory.

statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: rename Strand's 'Inspector' panel to 'Details' because Inspector is now a full view.
why: Avoids naming collision between a docked panel and a top-level view.

statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: the paper belongs to the workbook author — Classic draws a cell's own formats (including author red) as Excel draws them, keeping Strand signals in gutters, edges, overlays and chrome; provenance tints are an optional overlay in Classic and default dress in other views.
why: Prevents DNA Calc styling from corrupting author-formatted spreadsheets in Classic.

statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: add line style (solid, dashed, dotted) as a truth channel alongside Strand tenet 2's single border treatment.
why: Encodes stated vs inferred vs ghost status structurally without adding colours.

statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: warnings have no hue (bold ink plus hollow triangle) and saved or stale values use a diagonal hatch rather than a colour tint.
why: Preserves colour-channel discipline and legibility without colour vision.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: a skin may carry a theme, but a theme consists strictly of token values, must pass contrast checks, and cannot re-bind any semantic signal.
why: Allows visual customisation without weakening accessibility or signal honesty.

statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: cap the recalculation ripple at 400 ms total, stepping by block beyond 200 items, and do not animate a marching-ants copy outline.
why: Respects Strand's strict animation budget and prevents sluggishness on large sheets.

statement: Refinement to Strand v0.1: the agent has no dedicated hue of its own; its marks are teal, dotted and badged, never amber.
why: Keeps amber exclusively for the user's current selection and focus.

statement: Storyboard steps are numbered with exact keys and time budgets so they double as executable usability test scripts and requirement citations.
why: Ties narrative design directly to verifiable acceptance tests.

statement: First-run start page (M1.1) presents three verbs with keys (Open workbook Ctrl+O or drag-and-drop anywhere on the window, New workbook Ctrl+N, Formula Explorer Alt+Shift+E), a Recent list, a one-line compatibility promise ('Your file stays an Excel file. Nothing is added that Excel cannot open'), and the discovery rule ('Everything you know from Excel works in Classic. What is new is on Alt+Shift and Alt+Q').
why: Reassures cautious Excel users immediately and establishes the two-layer keyboard model on day one.

statement: Staged non-blocking open (M1.2): file name and sheet count appear in the Strip within 100 ms; the previously active sheet paints from saved values within 2 s for Inherited-scale files and is immediately scrollable/selectable while remaining sheets stream in; no modal dialogs interrupt for links, macros, or manual calculation—instead one non-blocking notice line summarises all notices and auto-opens the Overview panel with live 'so far' counts.
why: Eliminates Excel's startup dialog wall while keeping large files immediately responsive.

statement: When a workbook opens in manual calculation, nothing recalculates automatically; a hatched band marks values 'as saved <date> · not recalculated here · F9', error cells keep Excel's text with a red left tick, file macro buttons render and explain themselves when macros are off, and screen readers announce file name, sheet count, calculation mode, notice count, and F6 for Overview.
why: Prevents users from mistaking stale cached values for freshly calculated numbers.

statement: Pressing Alt displays Excel's exact key-tip letters on the Deck (and Q on the palette), honours paths typed from memory without waiting for tips to draw, shows digits 1-5 on the view tabs for Alt+Shift, and displays a one-line summary of the Alt+Shift layer on the first five uses of Alt.
why: Teaches DNA Calc's new shortcut layer in place through an existing Excel habit.

statement: From Overview › Errors, errors are grouped by root cause (e.g., 3 roots explaining 4,226 errors) with impacted cell counts; Enter jumps directly to the root cell, Alt+← (and browser Back) navigates back to the prior place, and Ctrl+C copies the root list as plain lines with addresses for email.
why: Turns thousands of cascading formula errors into a small actionable list.

statement: Model map at sheet zoom (Alt+Shift+4, within 150 ms) shows all sheets with the active sheet outlined in amber, missing external links in signal orange with dashed wires noting 'values as saved', standing counts per box (formula count, packed, errors), identical-formula sheets collapsed into a stack (e.g., Jan…Dec 12 alike), hidden/very-hidden/unread sheets explicitly counted in side buckets, and an accounting footer ('40 of 40 sheets accounted for · 62 links in 9 bundles · cells are not drawn at this zoom').
why: Gives an honest architectural overview of large workbooks without dropping sheets or shrinking text.

statement: On the Model map, semantic zoom (sheets · blocks · cells) keeps text at constant size; Ctrl+[ lights upstream wires one hop per press, hovering a wire bundle shows a peek card with reference count and example formula, Enter drills into a box (e.g., Curves as 6 blocks, never raw cells), Esc steps back out, and Space peeks at a hidden sheet under a non-mutating band ('Hidden in the file. You are looking, not unhiding').
why: Lets auditors inspect structure and hidden sheets safely without modifying the file.

statement: Clicking a workbook button when macros are off runs nothing and opens an inline card at the button naming the procedure, line count, and static summary of actions (e.g., opens 2 workbooks, copies 6 ranges, saves), with 'Read the code' and 'Allow macros this session' actions.
why: Explains macro refusals transparently in context instead of silently failing or forcing a blind enable prompt.

statement: Editing a cell sets the Mast state to 'edited', and undoing back to the file's opening content restores the Mast state to 'unchanged'.
why: Reflects exact workbook identity rather than a latched dirty bit.

statement: During manual recalculation (F9), the Strip turns amber with progress and 'Esc stops', the grid stays interactive while waiting cells remain hatched, and completion reports duration, how many values differ from the saved cache (linking to the diff list), and how many external links used saved values.
why: Keeps long recalculations interruptible and exposes silent drift from cached file values.

statement: Ctrl+wheel zooms the stage; below 40% zoom on packed sheets like Curves, unreadable cell text gives way to legible block outlines with labels, and high-contrast themes preserve the error tick, ◊ glyph, and hatch because each is a shape.
why: Preserves semantic legibility at low zoom and accessibility in high contrast.

statement: First-open value proposition for Excel users: no startup dialogs, explicit 'as saved' labelling, error counts reduced to root causes, read-only peeking of hidden sheets, and true 'unchanged' state after undo.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 1.

statement: On first visit to Notebook for a workbook without one (M2.1), the empty state offers a draft built from the program's reading ('By sheet, in order', 'Conclusions first', or 'Blank page'), lists what was read with a 'Why these?' link, confirms drafting changes nothing in the workbook, maps the active selection into the drafted outline within 400 ms, and states in the Strip where the selection landed while keeping Mast state 'saved'.
why: Avoids blank-page friction while proving that drafting is pure presentation (P4, P3).

statement: Reordering notebook sections via the Outline panel (F6, arrows, Alt+↑/Alt+↓, or drag handle) changes only presentation and updates the Mast state to 'saved, layout edited' to show the model is untouched.
why: Separates presentation edits visually from workbook model edits.

statement: Notebook text items (Alt, N, T) support inline live cell quotations (typing '=' and clicking a figure) that recalculate automatically, but refuse inline calculation expressions in prose with an inline offer to quote an existing cell or add the formula to the workbook.
why: Enforces P3 so no calculation ever hides outside the Excel model.

statement: Turning on the formula lens (Alt+Shift+L) renders defined names plainly and sheet-inferred labels inside guillemets (‹…›); right-clicking an inferred label offers 'Make it a name…' with a preview seam showing the Define Name and Apply Names scope; folded sections still surface run exceptions (e.g., 'People: 11 alike, 1 differs (Jun)').
why: Bridges readable labels and genuine Excel defined names while keeping exceptions visible.

statement: Editing a formula run item in Notebook (M2.2) edits all cells in the run (e.g., Monthly!C8:N8) as one formula with typo autocomplete suggestions, opens a dotted preview seam stating exact cell range, Excel formula text, result range, and whether values change, commits all cells as one undo step on Enter (exact revert on Esc), shows folded columns via a named control (◄ Mar–Nov ►), and propagates fresh marks through dependents and live prose quotations within 100 ms.
why: Prevents partial-row formula drift and makes multi-cell model edits safe from Notebook.

statement: Clicking a column header in a Notebook frame applies a labelled 'view sort ▲' that does not reorder the underlying sheet; copying a frame puts a formatted table for email and cells for Excel; pasting prose creates text items, while pasting an external table asks 'As text' (Enter) or 'As cells' with the exact target sheet range previewed.
why: Protects sheet data from accidental presentation sorts or unpreviewed pastes.

statement: Notebook 'Reading' density folds formulas to their names and sets prose in a serif reading face; Ctrl+P previews the write-up as a paginated document where each page footer carries the file name, active scenario, and value timestamp, and folded sections print as one-line summaries.
why: Produces director-ready narrative output tied verifiably to workbook state.

statement: Saving a workbook with a Notebook notifies once that it saved as an ordinary Excel workbook carrying the notebook inside (preserved and hidden by Excel) and sets Notebook (Reading density) as the workbook's preferred view.
why: Clarifies round-trip persistence for both DNA Calc and Excel recipients.

statement: Notebook accessibility: semantic headings map to real headings, formula items announce name, spoken formula, count and value range to screen readers, and at 200% zoom prose reflows while data frames scroll internally.
why: Meets screen-reader and low-vision zoom requirements without losing content.

statement: Notebook value proposition for Excel users: a row of twelve formulas behaves as one formula (preventing stragglers and surfacing existing ones), and prose figures stay live cell quotes that cannot drift from the model.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 2.

statement: When exactly two numeric cells are selected (e.g., clicking Report!D17 and Ctrl+clicking Report!D9), the Strip automatically adds their Difference alongside Sum and Count.
why: Eliminates scratch-cell subtraction during quick reconciliation.

statement: Ctrl+[ keeps Excel's exact jump-to-precedents behaviour; returning via Alt+← restores the selection and, once per session, the Strip gently offers 'Alt+Shift+T traces without leaving the cell'.
why: Guides Excel power users from familiar shortcuts to DNA Calc's Trace instrument.

statement: Trace panel (Alt+Shift+T, docking under the grid within 200 ms, M3.1) explains conditional aggregation formulas (like SUMIFS) as a ladder of criteria tests showing rows remaining after each test and rows that 'fail only this' test, displays graded diagnostic hints (e.g., '[!] Hint, likely: 41 rows carry a time of day'), and aggregates the flaw across the entire matching formula run (16 cells, 412 rows, 478,930.15).
why: Surfaces the exact near-miss rows where spreadsheet reconciliation bugs hide.
evidence: S3.3, M3.1; Sales Report!D9 vs D17

statement: Pressing Enter on a Trace ladder row opens the source table under a labelled non-mutating 'View filter from Trace' (M3.2) that leaves Excel's AutoFilter and SUBTOTAL untouched, marks gapped row numbers in teal with an omitted-row count, shows both formatted display and raw stored serial value in Details/peek card (exposing hidden time-of-day decimals), and clears cleanly on Esc.
why: Lets auditors inspect filtered failure rows and hidden stored precision without altering workbook state.

statement: Opening Formula Explorer on a cell (Alt+Shift+E) pre-populates its precedents and lets the user edit a trial formula ('Trying. Workbook unchanged.') to confirm a fix (e.g., changing '<='&D$4 to '<'&E$3) without modifying the file; Esc discards the trial.
why: Allows auditors to test formula hypotheses safely on a reviewer's copy.

statement: Switching from a docked Trace panel in Classic to full-stage Inspector (Alt+Shift+2) preserves the open trace and selected ladder node; returning to Classic (Alt+Shift+1) restores the active cell and scroll position.
why: Connects docked panels and the full Inspector view seamlessly.

statement: When typing in Classic would overwrite a formula inside a uniform run, the preview seam warns before commit ('Replaces a formula with text. Breaks a run of 16 alike'), and Esc reverts cleanly.
why: Catches accidental formula overwrites before they corrupt a sheet.

statement: Ctrl+Shift+F2 records a finding as a standard Excel comment, and Ctrl+C inside the Trace panel copies an audit-ready outline plus the filtered rows table for pasting into Word.
why: Produces standard Excel annotations and external audit documentation.

statement: Selecting a PivotTable displays its last refresh timestamp and whether its source data has changed since refresh in Details.
why: Makes PivotTable cache staleness immediately verifiable.

statement: The Trace conditional ladder is exposed to screen readers as an accessible tree announcing test index, criterion, remaining row count, and fail-only-this count.
why: Ensures full audit workflows work without sight.

statement: Trace value proposition for Excel users: unlike Evaluate Formula (which collapses SUMIFS in one opaque step), Trace explains row-testing functions row by row, lifts number-format disguises, and tests fixes without touching the file.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 3.

statement: Empty Model map (M4.1) teaches one grammar ('name = formula', e.g., Store.Initial = 400) and states that every box is a named cell on a visible sheet; typing on empty paper opens a preview seam showing the label cell, value cell, defined name, dotted-prefix inferred group frame (dashed because inferred), and a 'place it elsewhere…' option before commit.
why: Lets engineers sketch directly on the map while keeping every box standard Excel.

statement: Model map supports top-down sketching: within a prefix group (e.g., Store), short names resolve to that prefix (Stock -> Store.Stock); undefined names get dotted underlines and Enter offers 'Create empty boxes for both' or 'Commit as typed: Excel shows #NAME?'.
why: Supports whiteboard-style sketching without breaking Excel name semantics.

statement: While editing a box formula on the map (M4.2), clicking other boxes inserts their references and draws dotted ghost wires (whereas committed wires are solid and strictly derived from formulas); closing a circular loop while iteration is off presents an inline three-way choice at the box (turn on iteration with explicit Max 1 / 0.001 settings, keep without iteration as 0 with circular warning, or Esc back to editing) instead of Excel's modal dialog.
why: Turns circularity into an explicit, inspectable modelling decision.

statement: On a circular loop with iteration enabled, the frame displays an Excel-terms calculation chip ('iterates · 1 pass per recalculation'), a self-reference carries a certain delay mark [z-1], and a cross-box wire carries a delay mark only where the engine reports a last-pass read (C-21); if the engine cannot confirm, the loop is drawn with no delay claimed.
why: Enforces P1 honesty: never infer or fabricate a delay mark unsupported by evaluation order.

statement: Dragging the source end of an existing wire onto another box previews the exact formula reference rewrite ('In Store.Sales: Demand becomes Supply.Order', showing before and after formulas) and Esc cancels with zero change.
why: Makes visual rewiring map cleanly and safely to concrete Excel formula edits.

statement: Adding a Slider control on a map box (Alt, N, Control › Slider) previews adding a standard Excel scroll bar form control linked to the box's cell; dragging shows a ghost value and commits once on release so iterative models tick exactly once.
why: Prevents slider drags from triggering dozens of unintended iterative ticks while staying standard Excel.

statement: Pressing F9 steps an iterative model by one tick, animating amber through boxes in evaluation order before settling with fresh marks; the iteration chip offers 'Repeat F9, 4 per second', and any box can be pinned to Watch to plot its history.
why: Makes iterative dynamics observable in real time using Excel's native F9 calculation.

statement: Alt+Shift+0 opens Classic grid alongside the Model map (M4.3) with one shared selection and formula bar so edits in either pane update the other immediately, solid delay marks and calculation chips remain visible, the Strip continuously states calculation mode and tick count, and Alt+Shift+1 + Ctrl+` inspects every raw Excel formula full-screen.
why: Provides instant verification that the visual model is a plain Excel worksheet.

statement: Undo handles both model and per-view layout steps: Ctrl+Z in Map undoes a box drag as '(layout)', whereas Ctrl+Z in Classic skips Map layout steps because layout changes are invisible from the grid.
why: Prevents invisible undo actions in views that cannot see another view's layout.

statement: Saving a map-built workbook confirms that names, formulas, iteration settings and sliders are standard Excel while map layout travels in the file and is ignored by Excel, so F9 in Excel produces identical numbers.
why: Confirms full round-trip fidelity of map-authored models.

statement: Model map keyboard, screen-reader and clipboard rules: arrows move spatially, Ctrl+]/Ctrl+[ follow wires, Enter/Esc drill in and out, screen readers announce box name, role, value, inputs (including last-pass reads) and dependents, and Ctrl+C on a frame puts a picture for slides plus 'name = formula' text for editors.
why: Makes the graphical map fully operable without a mouse and interoperable with external tools.

statement: Model map value proposition for Excel users: circularity becomes a visible decision with settings on screen rather than a hidden dialog accident, and everything drawn is a readable standard Excel sheet.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 4.

statement: A workbook preferring App opens directly in App from saved values within 1 s, shows 'Checking the numbers' then 'Up to date' in plain Strip wording, hides the grid and formula bar by default, displays a one-time orientation note, and derives its input fields and limits automatically from unlocked cells, labels, and validation rules.
why: Gives non-Excel consumers an approachable calculator surface grounded directly in Excel features.

statement: In App, Tab visits editable white input fields only; committing a new value updates outputs, charts, and schedules within 100 ms with fresh marks and a 'was <opening value>' comparison caption.
why: Makes sensitivity exploration crisp and keeps the baseline figure visible.

statement: App layout and validation refusal (M5.1): Mast retains file, 'View as ▼' to every view, Print, and Ask (F6/Alt reveals Deck and Bridge); invalid entries are refused inline at the field using the workbook's own validation rule and message, offering Tab for a likely fix (e.g., 6.5% for 65) and Esc for exact revert; long schedules show a windowed frame with explicit counts ('360 payments · showing 3 · all ►').
why: Replaces jarring modal error boxes with contextual recovery while keeping full workbook access one click away.

statement: App scenarios (M5.2) bind directly to Excel's Scenario Manager: scenario chips switch inputs (and mark 'edited' when modified), 'Compare with: Base' displays Base values and deltas inline on every output tile (in-place Scenario Summary), 'Save as scenario…' previews which changing cells will be saved to Excel's Scenario Manager, and 'Reset' restores all inputs as one undoable step.
why: Makes Excel's underused Scenario Manager intuitive without inventing a proprietary scenario store.

statement: When an input causes a calculation error in App (e.g., Term = 0 causing #NUM!), every affected output tile shows the error code, red tick, plain-language cause from the trace root, and an 'Undo my last change' action—never a blank or stale number.
why: Enforces P1 honesty even in simplified consumer-facing App views.

statement: Resting on an App output tile reveals its provenance summary, cell address (e.g., Loan!C9), and 'See the cells (Alt+Shift+0)' so the underlying grid is always one key away.
why: Preserves auditability and trust without cluttering the App surface.

statement: Printing from App (Ctrl+P, page 1 previewed within 300 ms, M5.3) formats a clean one-page answer with optional Compare column, lets the user include/limit long schedules while stating page cost (e.g., 'all 180 payments, 4 pp' vs 'first year' vs 'none'), and adds a footer tying paper output to file name, scenario, and value timestamp.
why: Avoids accidental 40-page spreadsheet printouts while preserving provenance on paper.

statement: Closing a modified App workbook (Ctrl+W) summarises edits in plain words ('You added 1 scenario and changed 2 inputs') with Save, Save a copy, and Don't save.
why: Helps non-Excel users understand what saving will overwrite.

statement: App accessibility and touch readiness: rendered as a labelled form with live-region announcements for output changes, reflowing from two columns to one at 200% zoom, with controls at least 36 px tall for future touch use (though touch gestures are not designed yet).
why: Ensures accessible consumer usage and positions App as the first future touch target.

statement: App value proposition for Excel users: ordinary Excel habits (unlocked cells, validation rules, Scenario Manager) automatically create the App, while its end user sees zero cell references unless they ask.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 5.

statement: Standalone DNA Calc - Formula Explorer starts within 0.5 s into a clean workspace with one formula line (with faint example), a searchable function list, and immediate step-by-step evaluation beneath.
why: Provides instant zero-workbook formula testing.

statement: Loading an add-in via drag-and-drop or Alt, T, I presents a single trust card showing file path, build time, signature status, and permission warning ('Load once', 'Always trust this folder', 'Cancel'); once loaded, the Add-ins facet lists registered functions, descriptions, and authoring remarks (e.g., missing argument descriptions).
why: Balances security honesty with helpful developer diagnostics.

statement: In Formula Explorer, add-in functions appear in autocomplete marked with ◊ alongside registered signature and argument help, array outputs display as compact frames, and formula lines can be named ('spread = …') and reused in subsequent lines.
why: Enables multi-step formula and add-in testing without creating a worksheet.

statement: An 'Edge cases' palette command (M6.2) probes a function with awkward inputs (misspelling, wrong type, empty, error propagation, zero, out-of-range, range-for-scalar) with per-call timings; because add-ins run isolated, a crashing add-in shows a non-red warning '[!] add-in stopped' with exception details while keeping the Explorer and formulas intact, offering one-key 'Reload add-in' and 'Copy as a test case'.
why: Protects the host from add-in crashes and turns debugging into a fast loop.
evidence: S6.4, M6.2; Seasonal.xll division by zero

statement: Formula Explorer watches loaded add-in files on disk and offers one-key in-place 'Reload' without restarting the application, automatically re-evaluating all lines and marking changed results (e.g., 'was: stopped').
why: Eliminates Excel's restart penalty during add-in development.

statement: Formula Explorer includes Number format (previewing custom format codes across results plus positive, negative, zero, and text samples) and Conditional format (showing which rules fired on which values) facets.
why: Lets authors test formatting rules interactively alongside formula logic.

statement: Trusted add-ins are available in DNA Calc workbooks under Alt, T, I; when a dynamic array function hits a blocked spill (#SPILL!, M6.3), the needed extent renders as a ghost, and an inline card names the exact blocker cell and content, offers three actions (Go to blocker, Clear blocker, Move formula down one row), and notes that Excel will show #NAME? where the add-in is not installed.
why: Makes #SPILL! errors and add-in portability actionable right at the cell.
evidence: S6.7, M6.3; Monthly!C20:N20 blocked by N20

statement: Pressing Alt+Shift+E on a workbook cell opens Formula Explorer as a panel pre-filled with the cell's live inputs so users can override inputs in trial mode ('Trying. Workbook unchanged.') and Esc back cleanly.
why: Connects live workbook cells directly to safe isolated experimentation.

statement: Saving a workbook using an add-in adds a non-blocking Strip note ('◊ 1 formula uses Seasonal.xll. Excel shows #NAME? where it is not installed').
why: Keeps Excel portability caveats honest without blocking save.

statement: Formula Explorer clipboard interoperability: copying a formula line pastes into Excel as a formula and array results paste as values; pasting a formula from Excel into standalone Explorer turns its cell references into prompt inputs ('O14 = ?').
why: Bridges standalone testing seamlessly with real Excel workbooks.

statement: Formula Explorer keyboard and screen-reader design: F6 cycles formula line, inputs, result table and steps tree, Tab moves within regions, and array results are announced shape-first with min-max bounds.
why: Ensures full keyboard and screen-reader fluency in the Explorer.

statement: Formula Explorer value proposition: tests add-ins without a workbook, isolates crashes, hot-reloads rebuilds without restarting, and in the browser build honestly states that native add-ins cannot load.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 6.

statement: Free-form requests typed into the Alt+Q palette fall through to 'Ask the agent: …' as the last row; while running, the Mast shows agent reading status and the Strip offers 'Esc stops it' without blocking the user; the agent uses only the same addresses and commands as a human and routes writes into a proposal.
why: Unifies command search and agent invocation without creating a privileged back door.

statement: Agent proposals arrive in the Changes panel (M7.1) with nothing applied ('saved' untouched), split into independently tickable parts each quoting intent, exact cells, before (−) and after (+) formulas (using signs/words rather than red/green), pre-computed result impact ('no value changes' vs '8 results change'), and a 'Not proposed' note explaining rejected ideas; Space ticks parts, P enters a ghost preview on the stage (dotted `:val:` for unchanged, `a→b` for changed) under a preview band, and Esc exits preview.
why: Lets users verify exact model consequences part-by-part before anything touches the workbook.
evidence: S7.2, S7.3, M7.1; Budget Monthly!C6:N6, H13

statement: Ctrl+Enter accepts only ticked proposal parts, writing each accepted part as its own named step in the workbook's undo history.
why: Supports partial acceptance with clean per-part rollback.

statement: Undoing an accepted agent part via Ctrl+Z works from any view (e.g., Notebook), returns that part to pending in Changes rather than discarding it, and Undo History + Details › History (M7.2) distinguish model steps (filled dot) from layout/text steps (hollow dot), recording actor, timestamp, proposal/part, before/after formula, and cell-level provenance.
why: Makes agent edits first-class citizens in unified undo and audit trails.

statement: Pressing R rejects a proposal part with an optional reason; when rejecting an inconsistency fix, the cell becomes a noted exception that silences the run-break warning and optionally writes the reason as an Excel note (previewed and undoable).
why: Captures human domain rationale so neither the program nor the agent nags again.

statement: Out-of-order Revert restores an older step by writing a new forward undo step and refuses to clobber later edits to overlapping cells, naming the conflicting cell, actor and time with 'Show me' and 'Revert anyway' choices.
why: Enables selective rollback without silently destroying subsequent user work.

statement: Details › History on any cell provides long-term provenance showing who edited it, when, via which proposal, before/after formulas, and links back to the proposal and user notes.
why: Supports downstream audit weeks after an agent-assisted change.

statement: Agent permission boundaries: the agent may never change calculation settings, enable macros, load add-ins or save without explicitly asking; visual styling requests ('make Classic calmer') produce try-on skins that cannot touch formulas.
why: Enforces strict separation between model mutations, security/trust actions, and styling.

statement: Changes panel accessibility and clipboard: exposed as a checkbox list announcing part name, cell range, value-change impact and ticked state, and Ctrl+C copies a plain-text before/after summary.
why: Makes agent review fully accessible and shareable.

statement: Agent review value proposition: consequences on calculated values are computed before commitment, parts are accepted selectively, and accepted parts behave as standard Ctrl+Z undo steps.
why: Summarises the user-visible wins of Storyboard 7.

statement: Cross-storyboard coverage matrix maps eleven make-or-break UX moments (first run/empty states, feature discovery, loading/calc feedback, view switching, error/warning/refusal, undo/recovery, copy/paste, hover/focus/selection, perceived speed, accessibility, and Excel-user wins) to exact storyboard steps.
why: Verifies that every critical interaction class is exercised in concrete testable scenarios.
evidence: S1..S7, R-90, Section 6, Appendix A Part 12

statement: One shared pointer and one unified address grammar cover seven target kinds and are used identically by humans, macros, skins and agents.
why: Eliminates translation gaps between interactive UI, automation, skins and agents.

statement: Five of the seven addressable target kinds are native Excel objects using Excel syntax: cell/range (Monthly!H13, Inputs!C5:D16), spill (Monthly!C21#), defined name (ServicesShare, Store.Stock), table/column/row (Orders, Orders[Amount], Orders[@Date]), and named object (Loan!"Balance", Model!"Slider 1", Report!"PivotTable1").
why: Grounds addressing directly in standard Excel identifiers.

statement: Two non-Excel target kinds complete the address model: inferred blocks (addressed by range like Monthly!B5:O9 and displayed with ‹label› until pinned as a name) and pure presentation view items (addressed as view:notebook/Summary/text-1 or view:map/Store).
why: Gives inferred readings and presentation objects clean addresses without polluting the Excel model.

statement: Whenever a view item represents a model object, the address field displays the model address; for pure presentation items it displays the view path in muted ink and leaves the formula bar empty.
why: Keeps the boundary between model content and presentation immediately visible.

statement: Selection is stored in model terms and rendered on each view's finest containing item; when an item is coarser than the selection, the Strip explains the mapping and returning to a finer view restores the exact cells.
why: Preserves exact selection fidelity across views of differing granularity.

statement: Scroll and zoom state belong independently to each view and sheet; on view switch, the target view scrolls only as far as necessary to bring the selection into view.
why: Avoids jarring viewport resets when bouncing between views.

statement: Global navigation works in every view: F5/Ctrl+G/Name box/Alt+Q jump to any address, Ctrl+[/Ctrl+] traverse upstream/downstream, Alt+←/Alt+→ walk place history across sheets and views, and F6 cycles stage, companion, panel, Deck, Mast, and Strip.
why: Gives uniform spatial and dependency navigation across the entire workspace.

statement: At most two panes may be shown at once: a view and a companion (Classic grid by default) sharing the selection; free multi-pane tiling and separate tabs per view are explicitly rejected.
why: Free tiling causes users to get lost, and a tab per view hides that all views look at one workbook.

statement: Editing a non-grid item that stands for cells applies that edit to those cells (a run item writes to the first cell and fills across; a map box writes to its cell).
why: Guarantees direct semantic correspondence between view edits and Excel cells.

statement: Creating model content outside the grid follows the placement rule: write a label cell, a value cell, and (where the view works by names) a defined name in the next free row of its block/frame on a visible sheet, previewed and editable in the seam.
why: Keeps generated sheet layouts tidy, visible, and transparent to Excel users.

statement: Structural gestures outside the grid map strictly to Excel commands: rewiring replaces one reference with another, renaming a box renames its defined name, and deleting a box clears its cell and deletes its name while the seam lists every dependent that would turn #NAME?.
why: Ensures structural edits have exact Excel semantics and visible blast radius.

statement: Pure presentation edits (layout, order, folding, prose, view sort and view filter) are free, stored in the view part, and can never alter a workbook value.
why: Separates safe presentation authoring from model mutations.

statement: Any gesture outside the four legal edit categories is refused with a plain explanation and the nearest equivalent Excel can express.
why: Prevents inventing non-Excel semantics.

statement: Undo architecture: one shared model undo history per workbook plus a small presentation history per view; Ctrl+Z undoes whichever is more recent between the last model step and the focused view's last presentation step, with named steps (actor, action, target, cell count), macro runs and agent parts as single steps, workbook isolation, persistence across saves, 'unchanged' detection at open state, and conflict-checked Revert; one global stack and per-view model stacks are explicitly rejected.
why: A global stack would undo invisible layout drags from Classic; per-view model stacks would break chronological order.

statement: Errors are organised by root cause cell; Issues lists roots, cells show the red left tick, and containing boxes, notebook items, App tiles and sheet tabs inherit the red tick with a count.
why: Makes error origin and propagation visible at every zoom level.

statement: Every cell has one of five calculation states—fresh, settled, pending, stale (input changed under manual calc), or as saved—with the last three sharing the hatch; at workbook level the Strip reports mode, iteration settings, progress and last duration.
why: Makes calculation truthfulness explicit at both cell and workbook granularity.

statement: Outside data sources (linked files, RTD topics, volatile functions, add-ins) are first-class objects; cells they feed carry ◊, and Inspector › Live lists all sources with their live state.
why: Exposes external dependencies and live feeds as inspectable instruments.

statement: Typed warnings carry no colour hue and cover concrete conditions: run exceptions, numbers stored as text, pivots older than source, names using OFFSET, and missing external links.
why: Gives consistent, non-alarmist diagnostics distinct from red errors.

statement: The agent operates exclusively through the same addresses and commands as a human user (Strand tenet 7) with no private back door to the workbook model.
why: Guarantees uniform auditability and safety invariants for human and agent actions.

statement: Agent activity is shown via a Mast status chip (idle, reading where, working, proposals waiting) with no distracting stage cursor unless explicitly requested.
why: Keeps the user's stage calm while maintaining full visibility of agent work.

statement: Agent permission is configurable per workbook across three modes: Look, Propose (default), and 'Apply, then review' (which applies steps marked 'unreviewed' until kept or reverted via the same Changes panel and verbs).
why: Scales user control without multiplying review UIs.

statement: Every agent proposal part lists intent, target cells, before/after content, pre-computed result impact, and three automated checks (opens in Excel, adds no errors, breaks no run), with verbs tick, preview, accept ticked, and reject with note.
why: Gives reviewers objective evidence to accept or reject each part safely.

statement: Accepted agent parts become named undo steps in cell history; the proposal record stays with the session and optionally travels in the workbook file if the owner opts in.
why: Balances auditability with clean file defaults.

statement: High-impact actions (calculation settings, macros, add-ins, saving, sending data outside) are always asked rather than assumed, and visual/layout requests travel as try-on skins rather than model proposals.
why: Maintains strict trust and model/presentation boundaries.

statement: The clipboard carries the underlying semantic object (cells, value frame, or named box) rather than just pixels; paste behaviour adapts to destination view and previews any model-creating paste in the seam.
why: Makes copy/paste meaningful across views and external apps.

statement: Classic formula-pointing view (M8.1): each referenced range gets a superscript number and teal tone (no rainbow, no red) while the reference at the caret turns amber, the active cell mirrors the formula bar with caret, arrows move pointing and F4 cycles absoluteness, a function tooltip bolds the current argument with description, and the Strip displays Excel's 'Point' mode word.
why: Preserves full Excel pointing ergonomics while fixing colour-vision accessibility and red-signal reservation.

statement: Inspector view (M8.2) gives the stage to live instruments (Overview, Trace, Calc, Errors, Watch, Links, Names with live counts) that also dock as panels in every view; the Calc instrument records recalculations without storing anything in the workbook, displays Excel calc settings, lists cells in exact evaluation order with before→after values and last-pass read annotations (supplying the Map's delay marks), and plots watched values over ticks as a readout.
why: Makes execution order, iterative convergence, and state trajectories directly observable.

statement: Notebook 'Across' pipeline layout (M8.3) renders multi-stage workbooks left-to-right (Orders table frame with column types and freshly pasted rows → Report 16-cell formula run item with lens labels and hatched pending cells during live recalculation → PivotTable1 snapshot flagging '[!] Source changed after the last refresh' with Refresh Alt+F5).
why: Shows tabular data pipelines and calculation/cache freshness side-by-side.

statement: Model map at block zoom on an unnamed ordinary workbook (M8.4) draws inferred blocks as dashed frames with guillemet labels (‹Revenue›, ‹Costs›, ‹Result›) and real sheets as solid boxes, marks previous-period self-reads as [t-1] (deliberately distinct from iterative [z-1]), bundles wires with counts/names, surfaces run exceptions at every zoom, shows the active scenario switch on Inputs, and prints an exact accounting line.
why: Demonstrates that Model map works immediately on ordinary unnamed workbooks without manual wiring.

statement: Auto-drafted App page (M8.5) explicitly states 'drafted from the file · Edit page…', pulls inputs from the active scenario's unlocked column labelled from column A, compares every output tile against Base with numeric and percentage-point deltas, and draws workbook charts using distinct textures as well as tones for series comparison.
why: Delivers an instant executive comparison view while preserving colour-blind legibility and declarability.

statement: In-workbook Formula Explorer (M8.6) provides five facets (Steps, Functions, Number format, Conditional format, Add-ins), displays the stored cell formula beside an editable trial line ('Trying. Workbook unchanged.') with delta and 'Apply to cell (Ctrl+Enter)', lists cell precedents with shown and stored values plus 'try' override boxes, and evaluates every sub-expression (with row-count ladder for row functions).
why: Replaces Excel's cramped Evaluate Formula and Insert Function dialogs with a unified safe workbench.

statement: Standalone Formula Explorer (M8.7) carries its own identity badge (Strand dot-long pair), has no sheets/tabs/file, supports numbered optionally-named formula lines reusable below with optional leading '=', searchable built-in and ◊ add-in function docs, shape-first array result frames, the same five facets, explicit assumed cell context ('as if in cell A1 of an empty sheet · change…' for ROW/CELL), and 'Save as workbook…' exporting plain .xlsx.
why: Delivers a zero-friction formula/add-in calculator that upgrades cleanly into a standard workbook.

statement: Classic (Alt+Shift+1) is the default view for files without a stated preference, supports all Appendix A gestures, suits all five cast workbooks as the only never-summarised view, and does not suit explaining models to others or visualising Stock's feedback structure.

Inspector (Alt+Shift+2 or enlarging any instrument panel) uses ↑/↓, → expand, Enter navigate, Space pin to Watch, R record, F9 step; suits Inherited, Sales tracing, and Stock execution order; does not suit authoring or non-Excel consumers like Jo.

Notebook (Alt+Shift+3; first visit offers draft) uses ↑/↓ between items, Enter/F2 edit, Alt+↑/↓ move, Alt,N insert, → into values, Page/Across layouts; suits Budget, Loan explanation, Sales pipeline, Stock narrative; declines Inherited as a whole and offers a subset.

Model map (Alt+Shift+4; opens at the zoom showing ≤60 boxes) uses spatial arrows, Ctrl+[/] along wires, Enter in, Esc out, typing name=formula, wire dragging, pointing, +/- zoom; suits Stock, Inherited at sheet zoom, Budget at block zoom; collapses Loan's schedule and Sales' rows into single boxes by design.

App (Alt+Shift+5 or file preference; left via 'View as') uses Tab through inputs, Alt+↓ for lists/scenarios, Enter, Ctrl+P; suits Loan, Budget scenarios, Stock slider; does not suit Sales without a custom page and declines Inherited.

Formula Explorer opens via Alt+Shift+E, Shift+F3, Alt,M,V, or standalone; only 'Apply to cell' (Ctrl+Enter) writes; supports Enter evaluate, F9 partial eval, F4 reference cycling; suits any single formula and not whole-model exploration.
Touch and pen interactions are intentionally out of scope for now; when added, they will matter first in App (large inputs/sliders), then Model map (pen dragging boxes/wires), then Notebook (markup).
why: Focuses initial design on keyboard and pointer excellence.

statement: The formula lens (Alt+Shift+L in any view) alters display only—never storage—with three layers: Names (defined names plain, sheet-read labels in ‹…›), Layout (indented structural line breaks), and Steps (repeated sub-expressions shown once with notice 'shown as steps; stored as one formula'); typing accepts names/labels while previewing exact Excel text in the seam, hover shows plain references, and default is off in Classic and on in Notebook and Map.
why: Makes complex Excel formulas readable without inventing a non-Excel formula dialect.

statement: Reaction to names-in-motion and watershed previews: keep named boxes/reference wires, drill-in with breadcrumb, self-read delay marks, Presented/Excel lens toggle, evaluation-order ripple, group calc tags, and RTD event strip (as Inspector › Live); change palettes to Strand, replace 'Director' with Excel-terms calc chips, drop decorative motion while keeping value-carrying gauges, rename Stock⁻ to typeable/speakable Stock[last pass], and move the plotter to Watch.
why: Integrates proven preview strengths into Strand's honest, accessible design system.

statement: Mapping from the six earlier experimental views: Grid -> Classic, Notebook -> Notebook, Canvas -> Model map, Atlas -> Model map at sheet zoom + Overview, Tree -> Outline panel, and Ledger splits between Notebook frames and Inspector's Calc list.
why: Consolidates six experimental surfaces cleanly into five views and shared panels.

statement: Workbook readings carry three explicit evidence grades: Certain (stated in the file: tables, pivots, data tables, saved scenarios, form controls, validation, protection, names, print areas, iteration+loop, RTD/external refs, macros), Likely (structural: identical formula runs, steady period headers, constants read by formulas, matching sheet layouts, lookup shapes), and Guess (semantic: report sheet, running balance as stock).
why: Prevents heuristic guesses from masquerading as workbook facts.

statement: Reading evidence grades map consistently to line style (solid = certain, dashed = likely, dotted = guess); users can confirm or correct any reading in one gesture, corrections persist in the file's view part, readings never mutate the model, and no view blocks on confirming a reading first.
why: Keeps pattern inference lightweight, transparent, and non-blocking.

statement: An opened reading card (M9.1) displays kind, label, overall grade (the weakest supporting evidence grade), line-by-line evidence with individual grades, the nearest ruled-out alternative ('Not a table'), one-gesture presentation corrections (Rename, Change kind, Extend/shrink, Split, Merge, Not a pattern) accessible to both users and agents, and an explicitly labelled model-changing action ('Pin with a name…').
why: Makes inference explainable and one click away from user correction.

statement: Three composition rules govern overlapping patterns: a region may hold multiple readings simultaneously (e.g., time series + running balance + formula run), the highest-certainty reading governs default display, and exceptions inside any pattern are always surfaced rather than absorbed.
why: Handles realistic multi-pattern spreadsheets cleanly without hiding anomalies.

statement: Inherited.xls (40 sheets, 301,482 formulas, one sheet packed A1:IV900) is the benchmark workload for big-workbook rules and performance budgets.

Classic at scale: always shows every cell exactly via viewport virtualisation, never declines, replaces cell text with block outlines/labels below 40% zoom, and maps formula/error density in the scroll gutter.

Inspector at scale: shows lists up to 2,000 rows directly; above 2,000 groups errors by root and dependents by block/run with counts opened on demand; declines full million-cell precedent lists while showing blocks and offering Export or Narrow to one sheet.

Notebook at scale: shows sheets up to ~150 blocks directly, collapses runs to single items and frames to 20 rows with counts (keeping exceptions visible when folded, e.g., Curves as 6 items), and declines whole 40-sheet/1,907-block workbooks while offering one sheet, chosen outputs + feeders, or an outline.

Model map at scale: shows levels up to 60 boxes directly, stacks like sheets, bundles wires with counts, clusters blocks by region with 'x of y accounted for', and declines levels exceeding 2,000 items after clustering with filters (feeds selection, has errors, open as list).

App at scale: works cleanly on few marked inputs/outputs; with many candidates drafts from certain evidence only and lists remaining constants; declines unmarked massive workbooks like Inherited (2,300 constants) offering output-driven discovery or an agent draft.

Formula Explorer at scale: shows arguments up to 200 cells directly, summarises larger arrays by shape/type/first 20 rows while confirming results use all rows, and refuses formulas beyond Excel's limits in Excel's own wording.
Sampling is permitted solely for displaying windowed frames or argument previews, must always state 'showing n of N', and may never feed any calculated result.
why: Preserves exact Excel calculation results at all scales.

statement: Performance budgets target a current mid-range laptop; the browser build may take up to 2× longer only on startup and initial sheet-open budgets.
Budget: start to usable shell ≤1 s; standalone Formula Explorer ≤0.5 s.
Budget: open first paint of active sheet from saved values with usable grid ≤1 s (small workbooks) / ≤2 s (Inherited), with Strip progress within 100 ms.
Budget: all sheets reachable and Overview complete ≤5 s (small) / ≤8 s (Inherited), with nothing blocked meanwhile.
Budget: keystroke to echo aimed at ≤16 ms (≤50 ms worst case) in every view, even during loading and recalculation.
Budget: selection move and scrolling within one frame, never blank for longer than 100 ms.
Budget: commit to dependents shown ≤100 ms on small workbooks; on larger ones update the edited cell immediately, hatch dependents, show progress after 300 ms, and allow Esc interrupt.
Budget: view switch places selection within 150 ms and finishes within 400 ms (Inherited sheet map within 500 ms).
Budget: Alt+Q command palette opens in ≤50 ms and updates results within 50 ms per keystroke.
Budget: any operation taking >1 s shows progress and supports cancellation; any operation >10 s can continue in the background.

Release blockers that are never acceptable: UI hangs, dropping content without a stated count, or misstating the model in four specific ways—drawing an estimate as fact, showing a run as uniform when it has an exception, showing a saved/stale value as fresh, or drawing a wire absent from formulas.
why: Defines hard failure criteria for visual honesty and responsiveness.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: A skin is a named, code-free declaration.
why: Keeps file-carried skins safe to open without executing code.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can specify theme tokens (Strand token values, density, type sizes).

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can specify layout (open panels and docks, Deck tabs/commands, nine quick slots Alt+1..Alt+9, extra Strip readouts).

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can add keymap bindings freely and may override an Appendix A key only if announced visibly ('this skin departs from Excel in N keys').

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can define named sequences of existing UI commands that drive the interface and never mutate the model directly.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can arrange standard declarative panel parts (value, input, frame, chart, trace, text) bound to workbook addresses.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can store per-workbook and per-sheet view settings (preferred view, configured views, lens/overlays, notebook order/prose, map layout, App pages); unconfigured views remain openable via auto-drafting and say so.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skin declarations can store user corrections to inferred workbook readings.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Executable code is permitted only for new UI components (e.g., a new instrument), which must be installed like an add-in behind the same trust card and are never embedded in workbook files.
why: Enforces a strict security boundary between declarative skins and executable extensions.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Users author skins via Customise (Alt, W, U—drag panels, edit Deck, record commands, or edit text with live validation) and agents emit the exact same declaration format; every skin enters as a non-persistent try-on band ('Trying <name> · Keep · Edit · Discard (Esc)'), rule violations are rejected with plain reasons (e.g., red reserved for errors), and kept skins live with the user or workbook view part and share as a single text file.
why: Gives safe, reversible skin authoring for both humans and agents.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Fixed invariants no skin may alter: calculation and workbook content/formats, the five semantic signals and their shapes, Strip fixed readouts, the preview seam and Esc exact revert, the address grammar, trust cards, the return path to Classic grid, and contrast thresholds.
why: Protects core truthfulness, safety and accessibility invariants under arbitrary skins.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Example 1 ('Calm review' skin): an agent restyles Classic via declarative theme/gridlines/zoom/provenance-overlay/panels without altering workbook row heights, explicitly noting that row height is workbook formatting and would require a separate model proposal if desired.
why: Demonstrates the strict boundary preventing model edits from sneaking into skins.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Example 2 (Loan App page): an agent generates a declarative app-page from a three-line brief using workbook readings (inputs, headline, outputs, chart, 3-row expandable schedule, scenarios, print options), previews it via try-on (M5.1), saves it to the file as preferred view on Keep, and sends any suggested Define Name edits separately through Changes proposals so looks and model changes never mix.
why: Shows how declarative App authoring separates presentation try-on from model proposals.

statement: Classic prints identically to Excel (print areas, titles, page breaks, scaling, headers/footers, page order), previewed via Ctrl+F2 and Ctrl+P.
Inspector prints an audit-ready report of the active instrument (trace outline with values, errors by root, links list).
Notebook prints the document in reading order with windowed or full frames and folded sections as one-line summaries.
Model map prints the current zoom level on one page or tiled with legend and 'x of y accounted for' footer, plus an optional box-and-formula appendix.
App prints as a one-page answer with long frames optional and stating their page counts.
Formula Explorer prints a summary card showing formula, inputs, steps, and result.
Every print outside Classic carries a footer with file name, active scenario and value timestamp, and every view offers 'Print as Excel would'.

Existing VBA verbs keep their meaning across every view: Select/Activate/Application.Goto move the shared selection, MsgBox/InputBox/UserForms appear over any view, Application.StatusBar shows labelled in the Strip, and ScreenUpdating=False defers painting without hiding 'Macro running · Esc interrupts'.

Three new macro verbs (switch view, select by address, show/hide panel) are exposed via late-bound Application.Run ('DnaCalc.View', 'DnaCalc.Select', 'DnaCalc.Panel') so the same macro code fails harmlessly and can be stepped over in Excel.
why: Avoids breaking VBA compilation or workbook portability in Excel.

statement: Macros cannot dismiss a trust card, hide fixed Strip readouts, or change a skin; a view switch requested during an active user edit waits until commit.
A macro run is recorded as one named undo step (improving on Excel), macros default to off until allowed, and blocked buttons explain why they did not run.
Usability test protocol: participants receive the starting workbook and plain-language spoken task with no interface jargon and no coaching.
Usability script S1 (Excel power user on Inherited, 10 min): ≥8/10 name two error roots and missing links and state values are as saved; 0/10 believe it recalculated or froze.
Usability script S2 (Analyst on Budget, 15 min): ≥8/10 produce prose quoting a live cell and update 12 cells in one step; ≥9/10 correctly answer whether Excel will show the text.
Usability script S3 (Auditor on Sales, 8 min): ≥8/10 identify the time-of-day cause and show the 41 rows, with no stray edits surviving.
Usability script S4 (Engineer building Stock, 20 min): ≥7/10 build and step on F9; ≥9/10 explain where boxes live and what the delay mark means.
Usability script S5 (Manager with no Excel on Loan, 5 min): ≥9/10 print a scenario-labelled answer; 10/10 recover unaided from the 65% validation refusal.
Usability script S6 (Add-in developer, 15 min): ≥8/10 find the periods=0 failure, hot-reload without restarting, and resolve the #SPILL!.
Usability script S7 (Analyst reviewing agent proposal, 8 min): ≥8/10 accept parts A & B without leaving C applied; ≥9/10 accurately predict whether each part changes values.

Accessibility and comprehension verification: every script runs keyboard-only, at 200% zoom, and in high contrast; S2/S3/S5/S7 run with real screen-reader users; every script ends with a five-statement true/false comprehension quiz about the model (90% pass mark) to detect misleading views.
why: Directly tests whether any view misled the user about model truth.

statement: Mandatory screenshot review matrix: for every view across all 5 cast workbooks capture 8 states (at rest, selection+peek, mid-edit+seam, mid-calc/as-saved, error+root, lens on, agent ghost proposal, print preview) plus per-view Inherited limit, first-visit, 3 themes, 200% at 1280×720, and keyboard focus per control; any unproducible cell is a design gap.
why: Enforces completeness of visual states across every view.

statement: Push-back: Inspector as a separate view is only half the answer—tracing happens beside the data, so build instruments as dockable panels in every view first, with the Inspector view simply giving those same panels the whole stage.
why: A standalone-only Inspector view would rarely be visited during active work.

statement: Push-back: treating prose and reviewer findings as pure expendable presentation is too fragile because Excel hides custom XML and Document Inspector or file rewriters can strip it; keep the view-part default but offer an Excel-visible mirror (cell notes for findings, generated notes sheet for prose), treat the view part as rebuildable, and state this at first save.
why: Protects user-authored findings and narrative against silent loss in Excel workflows.

statement: Push-back: Model map should ship as a reader long before an editor—moving an existing reference or pointing during edit is well-defined, whereas dropping a new wire onto =A*B+C has no defined syntactic slot; ship reading/zoom/chips/ripple first, then rewiring/pointing, then blank-paper building, and never give wires semantics absent from formulas.
why: Avoids ill-defined graph editing that breaks Excel formula faithfulness.

statement: Push-back: per-sheet views should be a preference indicated by a tab badge rather than an automatic switch on tab click, because replacing the entire surface when clicking a sheet tab disorients users; apply preferences only when asked or once on workbook open.
why: Preserves spatial stability while still communicating sheet-level view affinity.

statement: Push-back: the formula lens must not invent LET or lambda structure by default because synthetic intermediate names can be mistaken for file content and blur what gets saved; default to name/label substitution and layout, make 'Show as steps' an explicit labelled mode, and make 'Rewrite as LET' an explicit previewed model edit.
why: Prevents display syntax from lying about stored workbook formulas.

statement: Push-back: standalone Formula Explorer 'with no workbook at all' still needs named values, small arrays, and session persistence; provide no workbook chrome, but let lines and inputs save as a plain .xlsx with no new proprietary file type.
why: Makes standalone testing practical for non-scalar formulas without inventing a new format.

statement: Risk: the long tail of Classic Excel conformance where every missing gesture feels like a bug. Mitigation: treat Appendix A as a tiered executable checklist and put 'Report a difference from Excel' in the palette.
Risk: wrong workbook readings appearing authoritative. Mitigation: encode confidence grades in line style, keep evidence one gesture away, and never trigger a model change from a reading alone.

Risk: the view part is fragile—Excel or tools can strip it and external edits can make anchors stale. Mitigation: anchor to visible names/tables where present, else address + label/formula fingerprint, re-match with notice on open, and retain unmatchable items as noticed orphans.
Risk: proposal fatigue when reviewing agent edits. Mitigation: show computed value effects first and never pre-tick any part that changes calculated values.
Risk: Inherited-size files overwhelming the browser build. Mitigation: enforce section 6 speed budgets as release criteria and design declining states up front.

Risk: browsers intercept Excel shortcuts (Ctrl+N/T/W/Tab, etc.). Mitigation: provide an installed app window mode capturing them, document alternates, and state every difference transparently (Appendix A Part 12).
Risk: five views feeling like five disconnected products. Mitigation: one shell, one selection, one formula bar, and never more than two panes.
Risk: native add-ins and macros failing on platforms that cannot run them. Mitigation: clear refusals, marked saved values, and a path to open on desktop.

Open question on hidden defined names as view anchors: Fable recommends NO—use visible names/tables and fingerprints with user-initiated 'Pin with a name', because hidden names violate the rule that every model change is visible and user-reproducible.
why: Avoids silently polluting Excel workbooks with hidden names.

statement: Open question on persisting agent change trails in the file: Fable recommends OFF by default, opt-in per workbook, storing only a structured summary (who, when, proposal, cells) rather than full transcripts.
why: Balances audit trail availability with file cleanliness and privacy.

statement: Open question on where map-created boxes live: Fable recommends named cells on a user-named visible sheet (label + value in two columns, shown in seam) rather than formula-only names, because state, charts, controls and Excel audit tools all require cells.
why: Ensures map-authored models are first-class Excel sheets.

statement: Open question on add-ins and macros in browser builds: Fable recommends desktop-only initially, showing saved values with ◊, a one-line reason, and 'Open in the desktop app' in the browser.
why: Keeps browser behaviour honest where native execution is unavailable.

statement: Open question on key-tip letter parity with Excel: Fable recommends YES, holding key-tip letters in a path table independent of Deck styling because letters are behavioural muscle memory rather than Microsoft artwork.
why: Preserves Classic keyboard muscle memory without copying Office visuals.

statement: Milestone 1 (Shell and Classic core): Mast, Deck with key tips, Bridge, truthful Strip, Appendix A Tier 1, staged opening within budget, unified addresses, named undo (tested by S1.1–S1.3, S1.7–S1.9).
Milestone 2 (Reading the file): blocks, runs, grades/corrections, Overview, Issues by root, Trace and Details panels, place history (tested by S1.4, S3).
Milestone 3 (Formula Explorer and lens): in-workbook and standalone Formula Explorer plus first two lens levels (tested by S6, S3.5, S2.4).
Milestone 4 (Notebook): draft, run items, frames, prose with live quotes, Reading density, print (tested by S2).
Milestone 5 (Changes and skins): proposals with pre-computed effects, per-part acceptance, Revert, cell history, declarative skins with try-on (tested by S7, §7 example 1).
Milestone 6 (Model map): reader first (levels, stacks, bundles, chips, ripple), then rewiring/pointing, then empty-paper building (tested by S1.5, then S4).
Milestone 7 (App): drafted inputs/outputs, Excel scenarios, compare, print, declarative pages (tested by S5, §7 example 2).
Milestone 8 (Inspector bench, hardening): Calc recording, Watch, Live, Inherited against every budget, coded components (tested by S3.6, §6).

Milestone ordering follows two rules: every milestone must be independently useful to at least one persona, and truth-telling instruments (Milestones 1–2) precede summarising views (4, 6, 7) so every simplification points back to an exact view.
why: Ensures incremental value and grounded verification throughout delivery.

statement: Classic keyboard and mouse conformance contract: every listed gesture matches Excel for Windows (US keyboard), tiered into T1 (first release) and T2 (follow-on); deliberate differences are enumerated in Part 12 and any unlisted divergence is a bug.
why: Establishes an objective, testable parity standard for Classic.

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-3
statement: Classic conformance A-3 (T1): Double-click a cell — Edit, with the caret where clicked. If in-cell editing is switched off in options, the double-click goes to the cell's precedents instead.
why: Required for Excel for Windows parity (T1).

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-4

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-5

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-6

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-8

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-9

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-10

why: Required for Excel for Windows parity (T1).

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-11
statement: Classic conformance A-11 (T2): Insert, in Edit — Toggles overtype.
why: Required for Excel for Windows parity (T2).

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 1. Modes and entry) A-12

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 2. Committing, cancelling and what an entry means) A-13

source: pro19-fable/answer.md Appendix A (Part 2. Committing, cancelling and what an entry means) A-14
